content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a network-building method by using a linear combination of many randomly-generated models. It can build highly-compressed network with improve accuracy than other networks
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength
  - Due to the fact that just small amounts of seed values are stored in memory, this method can achieve remarkable compression ratios.
  - This paper also shows the improved performance of many networks than other highly-compressed networks. 


- Weakness
  - The performance is not enough to utilize for practical applications. While most of the results are evaluated by using small datasets (CIFAR-10 / tinyImageNet), the networks are too big than datasets (i.e. redundant models). Moreover, AlexNet is too old to discuss the novelty of current networks (10th anniversary?).  Although this paper shows more improved results than other compact networks, the absolute levels of performance are too low. It means that it is hard to evaluate the performance of this method.
  - This compact model can be utilized for an unusual situation (e.g.  limited resources, small devices, …). Then, this paper should also provide the environmental assumptions or applications to describe their performance of this method. I don’t know whether this method works very well or not.
  - This paper’s goal is to build compact models with few parameters. However, if their method can only produce poorer performance than benchmark models, I should raise this question, why should we use deep neural networks to solve problems?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I don’t want to raise issues on clarity and reproducibility. I think this method is clear and easy to reproduce by readers. But, in the aspect of quality and novelty, they should provide other advanced experiments to prove the novelty of this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I have been interested a lot in similar ideas such as randomly-generated weights, which can achieve huge compression ratios because we just need to memorize the seeds for random generation h/w or s/w libs. It would solve the memory-bound problem of large DNNs. But many researchers have failed in developing such networks or methods because absolute accuracy of such compact networks has not been satisfied in the aspect of practical requirements. We can implement compact networks with ultimately high compression ratio using a limited number of channels/layers or compression ideas. But, it is hard to push the accuracy of such networks over minimum criteria.

I think this paper implements similar networks with insufficient performance. I really agree that the idea of using a random-number generator is so useful if we could find the applications with adequate performance with that. However, this paper’s accuracy results are not sufficient to meet our service requirements. It must be not useful for real applications.

content.title: Addressing Concerns
content.comment:
We focus on large compression factors. We agree that the accuracy drops, but we believe it is fair to compare with baselines with similar numbers of parameters. We show that our method outperforms all such baselines using a smaller number of parameters.

We have focused on developing the reparameterization method and believe experimenting with a specific application is out of the scope. 

In our recent experiments, we show that our framework can compress an image by compacting an implicit neural representation (INR) model that is overfitted to a single image. Then, one can communicate or store the alpha values, so that it can reconstruct the INR and produce the image. We show that our method outperforms JPEG compression in PSNR and MS-SSIM metrics on Kodac Dataset.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an alternative model training approach that initializes many random models and then learns how to linearly combine these random models for the best performance. The authors show the advantages of this approach in reducing the storage size of the final model (linear combination of random models) since storing a random seed and a scalar per basis model is enough. The authors compare their proposed approach with data distillation and pruning methods on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet-100 datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is well-written and clear. 
- Learning a good linear combination of random networks is a novel idea, as far as I know.

Weaknesses:
- While the idea is novel, it is not clear when we can find a good linear combination of k models to achieve a good performance on a certain task is not clear. Is there any study showing the existence of a good linear combination under some conditions? 

- As the authors acknowledge, the proposed scheme increases the memory cost significantly since k-many models need to be stored during training. The authors propose a few remedies for this, such as training the weights of only m (m<k) models at each iteration. I don't think this is a practical solution because this requires reconstructing m random models every iteration, increasing the computational cost. Besides, updating only a portion of $\alpha$ would output suboptimal solutions and can potentially impact the performance of the final model. The authors should perform additional experiments to show how decreasing m from k affects the accuracy of the model and speed of training.

- It is not clear how precise the learned $\alpha$ should be communicated or stored. Are we assuming 32 bits representation? 

- The statement "quantization has the limit of (32 x) size reduction by reducing the 32-bit floating point to binary" is not true. Many quantization works proposed vector quantization methods (and variations of them) that go beyond 1 bit. I strongly suggest the authors fix this claim and acknowledge prior work that goes beyond 1-bit using variants of vector quantization such as SuRP[1] and DeepCABAC[2]. They provide up to ~300x bitrate improvements as opposed to the paper's claim of 32x limitation. 

- On page 5, the authors refer the reader to Table 3 for dataset distillation results, but I think it should be Table 1?

- It is not clear to me what #Params represents in Table 1. I assume for the proposed method, #Params is the number of base models. Please correct me if I am wrong. But I am not sure what #Params means for the dataset distillation baselines in Table 1.

- I do not understand why the authors choose to compare the proposed method against dataset distillation methods. There is also some comparison against pruning baselines, but the dataset distillation results are much more extensive. Is there a reason why the authors focused on this comparison? 

- I also find it bizarre that the authors emphasize that the goal is to make the storage of the final model more efficient and yet they compare their method against pruning and distillation works but not against quantization papers that actually try to minimize the bitrate. Comparisons to SuRP[1], DeepCABAC[2], MRC[3] etc. would provide a more meaningful justification for the paper's claims.

- For the comparison to pruning, the authors choose two pruning papers, neither of which has any specific strategy to encode the pruned model efficiently. In contrast, there are more recent works that have efficient ways of encoding a sparse model. For instance, SuRP[1] minimizes the size of the model while sparsifying it jointly. DeepCABAC[2] first sparsifies the model and then encodes the sparse model. Even the relatively older work Deep Compression [4] mentions Compressed Sparse Row format to encode the pruned model rather than simply encoding the index and the value of weight as mentioned in this paper. So, the authors should correct their statements about the current state of encoding a pruned model and show comparisons to the more relevant prior work [1,2,4].

- What does (1,376) correspond to in Table 3?

[1] Isik, Berivan, Tsachy Weissman, and Albert No. "An information-theoretic justification for model pruning." International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. PMLR, 2022.

[2] Wiedemann, Simon, et al. "Deepcabac: A universal compression algorithm for deep neural networks." IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing 14.4 (2020): 700-714.

[3] Havasi, Marton, Robert Peharz, and José Miguel Hernández-Lobato. "Minimal random code learning: Getting bits back from compressed model parameters." arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.00440 (2018).

[4] Han, Song, Huizi Mao, and William J. Dally. "Deep compression: Compressing deep neural networks with pruning, trained quantization and huffman coding." arXiv preprint arXiv:1510.00149 (2015).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear, and the main idea seems novel. The authors share the code for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: I like the originality of the main idea. However, I have some concerns about some of the claims, the baseline selections, and the lack of justification for some of the claims. I am happy to increase my score if the authors address my concerns.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Addressing Concerns
content.comment:
We have not done any study to show when this reparameterization is possible. We believe this is out of the scope of this paper.

$\textbf{the memory cost}$: updating a random subset of alpha values is a variation of standard coordinate descent algorithm which is known to converge. In our new code, to reduce the memory footprint, we divide the base network matrix $\hat{\theta}$ into smaller chunks and generate and then discard each chunk at the GPU for each iteration of the optimization. We observe that the overhead of generating the random matrix many times is negligible leading to reducing the memory footprint by a large factor due to not storing the random matrix.

We used 32-bit precision for alpha values, but in our newer experiments, we use half-precision for alpha values and do not see any degradation in performance.

$\textbf{quantization has the limit of (32 x) size reduction}$: Yes, we agree. Thanks for pointing it out. We will remove this statement.

Yes, we report the number of base models as the number of parameters since each base model has a single scalar coefficient. Data distillation methods compress the training data, so one can communicate or store the smaller dataset only to train the model again. We count the number of parameters in the distilled dataset: size of each image times the number of images.

We do extensive comparison with data-distillation methods since they reduce the number of parameters that can be stored to reproduce the model later. We perform more extensive comparison with other methods including network pruning ones in the newer version.

Thanks for pointing out the quantization papers. In recent experiments, we did compare with SuRP and outperformed it by a large margin. For instance on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20 and almost 1000 parameters, we are getting 64\% while SuRP gets 54\%.

(1,376) in Table 3 corresponds to the number of parameters of the BatchNorm layer. Since the mean and variance are calculated from the data and are not learnable parameters, we do not include them in our PRANC framework so we need to store or communicate them. Hence, we have added them while separating with parenthesis.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper suggests a model compression approach of using \theta = \sum \alpha_i \theta_i where \theta_is are randomly initialized and are fixed and we can learn \alpha_is only. As a result all \{ \theta_i \} can be represented by a single SEED and storage cost is (k +1) where k is the number of \theta_is. 

**Major questions.**
1. The work does not talk about a very important and very relevant model compression approach of parameter-sharing especially, Chen 2015 (1200 citations, http://proceedings.mlr.press/v37/chenc15.pdf ) . In fact, i believe that the method proposed in this paper is exactly the method proposed in the Chen 2015. We can consider authors method as follows 
\theta = T \alpha
Where T is the matrix where columns are all theta_i and alpha is the vector of all alphas.
In Chen 2015, they use where S is generated as a sparse matrix which is a simplification for efficiency over, say, gaussian matrices.
\theta = S \alpha
So the proposal looks exactly the same. 
            It is thus even more important to understand what distribution over S(or T) do you use and if that helps / hurts in your case. 
I would like to know the author's thoughts on this similarity between the two works?
As a side point, the authors should consider adding a literature review on parameter-sharing methods and contrasting their method with this. As far as i know, parameter sharing has shown high compression rates in fields like recommendation.

2. What is the distribution from which \theta_i s are generated ?


**Detailed questions.**

1. Section 5, page 8. Given that the alphas are learned, how can we sort the alphas ? Is this done as post training investigation? If so, how can it be leveraged in actual training ?
2. Page 6, Minor seed change experiment. Can you please shed some light on the importance of this experiment. In attacks on secure networks, is it more probable to recover a nearby number for seed than faraway number?
3. Page 6, What is the #parameters for data-distillation results ?
4. Page 4 "For large models, all the basis models may not fit in the GPU ...". Why do we need to realize all the basis models. We just need to compute the final model \sum(\alpha_i \theta_i) which can happen in O(d) memory by generating weight on the fly" then compute the f(\theta) and do the update to \apha as proposed in paragraph "optimization efficiency"
5. Page 3 “in contrast to goal of prior work … aim to reduce inference computation…” , I believe the aim of model compression is very much in line with the goal of your paper which is to create compact models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well written and easy to understand and well motivated. For weaknesses, please consider the above questions in summary.
Weaknesses:
1. The experiments are restricted to very small size of alpha (10K / 30k) which are either not very useful or cannot be directly compared to other methods like hashednets. 
2. The results on CIFAR etc are a bit inconclusive because we know higher accuracies 94% can be achieved with simpler ResNet mode. So if a compressed model can reach 81% is that really good? We dont know. If we use alexnet and see it reaches 84% then it will seem so . But its hard to judge these results
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written. The evaluation has some flaws  ( see weaknesses) . And the strong similarity to Model compression ( hashedNet style compression) limits the novelty of the paper. There is value in the point of view taken by the paper - linear combination of random vectors and I strongly encourage the authors to look deeper into this.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The major concern as expressed in questions in summary is that model compression by parameter sharing is a well explored area and has shown good results recently. Given that this work was not cited and not compared against is a definite concern. As it is a very close baseline the only difference being initialization of thetas. 

Other Suggestions (apart from the ones above) 
1. It might be interesting to contrast the method against other methods on randomized neural networks. One work that comes to mind is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/cao22a/cao22a.pdf. I am sure there are others. 

2. The comparisons that are done in the paper are done on some really small size of alpha (10K or 30K) even for models which have 11M parameters. Ideally a large range of alpha should be considered. It will give the readers more confidence on the method.

3. Model compression is very sensitive to the accuracy of the baseline models on the dataset and initial redundancy for the model. The results on CIFAR etc are a bit inconclusive because we know higher accuracies 94% can be achieved with simpler ResNet mode. So if a compressed model can reach 81% is that really good? We dont know. If we use alexnet and see it reaches 84% then it will seem so . But its hard to judge these results. I would advise using benchmarks (for example, DawnBenchmark, etc there might be more) which are fast implementations for a reasonable accuracy ( it reaches 94% accuracy in small number of epochs)
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Addressing Concerns
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for pointing out our HashedNet. We missed and will cite that one and relevant work in the next version. 

HashedNet can be seen as a specific case of our method where the random models are binary, each random model has an equal number of ones, and each weight of the original model is one only in one of the random models. The original HashedNet paper experiments with MLP on MNIST. We reproduce it for our setting and show that our method outperforms it. On ImageNet-100 with ResNet18, HashedNet archives 52.96\% with 129,200 parameters while PRANC achieves 61.08\% with 119,200 parameters.

We sample base networks from an i.i.d. normal distribution.

Questions:

1. Yes, the sorting is done offline only to show that larger values are more important in reconstructing the model. We do not leverage that in learning, but one can add $\ell_1$ regularizer to enforce sparsity.

2. A little change in the seed of the random generator will result in generating totally different random numbers, which will reconstruct a totally wrong model. We show that this model has an accuracy close to chance.

3. Data distillation methods compress the training data, so one can communicate or store the smaller dataset only to train the model again. We count the number of parameters in the distilled dataset: size of each image times the number of images.

4. Yes, you are right. In our new code, to reduce the memory footprint, we divide the base network matrix $\hat{\theta}$ into smaller chunks and generate and then discard each chunk at the GPU for each iteration of the optimization (once for forward and once for backward pass). We observe that the overhead of generating the random matrix many times is negligible leading to reducing the memory footprint by a large factor due to not storing the random matrix.

5. Yes, we agree.

Strength And Weaknesses:


1. We are more focused on compression with very small budgets.

2. We agree that changing the model architecture can achieve better results, but changing the architecture is either manual like ResNet or automatic, which is a different research area. Our method is an automatic way of reducing the number of parameters for a given architecture.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed a method to use the weighted sum of a bunch of random tensors as the weights for a DNN, to compress the storage needed for saving and reconstructing a DNN for actual inference.

The proposed method mainly targets on reducing the communication cost (by reducing the bytes needed for transmission), the mode storage, and run-time memory for inference (by generating weights of each layer on the fly).

The experiments results show that using 1~20 K parameters, the proposed method can get better accuracy compared to dataset distillation methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- This paper proposed a novel approach to use the random seed encode a random network, then use a bunch of learnable coefficients to do a weighted sum of these random networks and reconstruct a DNN which can be used for inference.
- The proposed method has very good compression ratio: one random seed can encode an entire DNN, and the final accuracy can be better and better by increasing the number of random DNNs.
- Experiments shows that under extreme compression rate, the proposed method can give better accuracy than dataset distillation methods and several DNN pruning methods.

Weaknesses
- Although one random seed can generate a whole DNN, the process of this generation may not be efficient. From the results, we can see that the number of random DNNs needs to be relatively large to get a reasonable results (e.g., 10K). While it is not efficient to reconstruct a DNN from this number of DNNs.
- From the experiment results, the accuracy of the weighted-sum DNN is still having a large gap to the standalone model. It's not clear if this large accuracy gap can be applied in practice.
- Although communication cost is reduced a lot in the training, the computation is increased heavily, e.g., (10k * num of parameters for averaging on each forward).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and easy to understand.

The paper proposed a novel direction to compress the DNN weights by using random seed, while the final accuracy gap to standalone model is too large, and there is no novel techniques proposed to mitigate this gap.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposed a novel direction to compress the DNNs using random seed and random number generator.

The compression rate is great, while results in large accuracy gap to standalone baseline model.

In addition, the computation cost of the proposed method is larger than standalone baseline and it's not clear if this computation cost would be an issue though the storage is saved.

content.title: Addressing concerns
content.comment:
We agree that model reconstruction is expensive since it involves linearly combining many random models. However, this is a one-time cost and after reconstruction, we can run many forward passes at the same cost as a regular model. We focus on compactness and not computational efficiency.

Yes, our method reduces accuracy compared to the full model that has a much larger number of parameters, however, it is fair to compare with baselines with the same compactness. We do this and show that our method outperforms the baselines with a large margin.

In our recent experiments, we show that our framework can compress an image by compacting an implicit neural representation (INR) model that is overfitted to a single image. Then, one can communicate or store the alpha values, so that it can reconstruct the INR and produce the image. We show that our method outperforms JPEG compression in PSNR and MS-SSIM metrics on Kodac Dataset.
